name: Kansas
tagline: From tallgrass Flint Hills and red Gypsum Hills to chalk badlands and Route 66.
intro: Kansas's byways cross the tallgrass Flint Hills and the red Gypsum Hills, follow old military roads and the Pony Express line, and run out to the chalk badlands and grain country near Colorado. This chapter follows the Kansas Byways Program, promoted by Kansas Tourism, with each route designated by the Kansas Department of Transportation. The state counts 13 byways, nine scenic and four historic, and two of the scenic ones, Flint Hills and Wetlands & Wildlife, are also National Scenic Byways.

members.name: Flint Hills National Scenic Byway
members.blurb: K-177 runs 47 miles from Council Grove south to Cassoday over open tallgrass hills, past the bison herd of Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve and Cottonwood Falls, whose 1873 courthouse is the oldest still working in Kansas.

members.name: Frontier Military Historic Byway
members.blurb: Some 168 miles from the Oklahoma line to the gates of Fort Leavenworth along the Army's old supply road, by way of the 1842 post at Fort Scott and the Mine Creek battlefield of 1864.

members.name: Glacial Hills Scenic Byway
members.blurb: K-7 runs north from Fort Leavenworth through the Missouri River town of Atchison and on to Troy and White Cloud, over rolling hills and rock-strewn valleys left by ancient glaciers, with a short jog onto county roads near Troy.

members.name: Gypsum Hills Scenic Byway
members.blurb: US 160 crosses 42 miles of red-earth buttes and mesas between Medicine Lodge and Coldwater, ground stained by iron in old Permian beds and pocked with sinkholes where gypsum has dissolved underneath.

members.name: Land and Sky Scenic Byway
members.blurb: K-27 runs 88 miles north from Sharon Springs through Goodland to the Nebraska line across open grain country, ending near the Arikaree Breaks, a band of water-cut loess ravines on private land.
members.note: Route line from the state route layer (not in the 2022 national dataset).

members.name: Native Stone Scenic Byway
members.blurb: About 75 miles of K-4, K-99 and K-18 through the northern Flint Hills, past stone barns and limestone fences to Alma, the WPA-dug Lake Wabaunsee and the Beecher Bible and Rifle Church at Wabaunsee.

members.name: Kansas Pony Express Historic Byway
members.blurb: From Troy west to the Hollenberg station near Hanover, 122 miles of US 36 and back roads through Marysville, where a limestone barn of 1859 is the only Pony Express home station left on its original site.
members.note: Route line from the state route layer (not in the 2022 national dataset).

members.name: Post Rock Scenic Byway
members.blurb: K-232 runs 18 miles from Lucas to Wilson beside Wilson Lake and across its dam, through pasture still marked by fence posts of quarried limestone, to the World's Largest Czech Egg in Wilson.

members.name: Prairie Trail Scenic Byway
members.blurb: From Ellsworth past the sandstone mushrooms of Mushroom Rock State Park and the canyons at Kanopolis Lake, then east through Swedish Lindsborg and on county roads to Canton, about 80 miles in all.

members.name: Kansas Historic Route 66 Byway
members.blurb: Thirteen miles of the old Mother Road from Galena through Riverton to Baxter Springs, crossing Brush Creek on the 1923 Rainbow Bridge, the last Marsh arch left on Route 66, through old mining country.

members.name: Smoky Valley Scenic Byway
members.blurb: A 60-mile horseshoe south from WaKeeney on US 283 and back north on K-147 to Ogallah, around Cedar Bluff Reservoir and its limestone bluffs, near the canyon where stage-trail travelers carved their names.

members.name: Western Vistas Historic Byway
members.blurb: US 83 north from Scott City past the El Cuartelejo pueblo ruins at Lake Scott and the white chalk canyons of Little Jerusalem, then US 40 west from Oakley to Sharon Springs and the Fort Wallace cemetery.

members.name: Wetlands & Wildlife National Scenic Byway
members.blurb: Some 77 miles of state and county roads from Hoisington to St. John join the marshes of Cheyenne Bottoms and Quivira, where waterfowl and shorebirds, and now and then whooping cranes, stop over on the Central Flyway.
